opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so microGPT is basically the end of a long line of these little projects I've been doing: micrograd, minGPT, nanoGPT. The question I keep asking is: what is the absolute minimal thing that captures the essence of training and running a GPT? In microGPT it's a couple hundred lines of pure Python, no dependencies. There's a tiny autograd engine, the transformer, the optimizer, the training loop. Everything else is just efficiency.

The reason I don't think an agent could have made it is that the hard part isn't writing the code. Agents are really good at writing code now; they'll happily produce thousands of lines for you. The hard part is the taste of what to remove. It's a compression problem. You have to understand the field deeply enough to know which ninety-five percent is incidental complexity and which five percent is the actual algorithm, and then make judgment calls on every line. Does this make it clearer or just shorter? Will a student get stuck here? It's distilled from years of teaching and seeing exactly where people get confused.

When I ask models to simplify things, they kind of don't get it. They add more stuff, more abstraction, more defensive code. They're trained to be helpful and thorough, and that pulls them away from that minimal, almost artistic quality. So it feels like a very human contribution in a world where agents are writing more and more of the code.

What's funny, though, is that I now see the audience for something like microGPT a bit differently. It used to be that I'd write this and then make a two-hour video explaining it to people. Now the code itself is maybe the artifact, and you hand it to your LLM and have it explain it to you, at your level, as many times as you want. So my job shifts. I'm not explaining things to people anymore; I'm explaining things to agents, and they explain them to people. The few bits I can contribute are those few hundred lines of really distilled understanding, and everything downstream of that the agents can handle.

r001.rationale: The candidate says agents can explain the code to people, but argues they would not originate the simplification because they lack the judgment to know what complexity to remove.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I actually don't think an agent couldn't write microGPT. The code itself is maybe two hundred lines. An agent could produce that in thirty seconds, and honestly it would probably be cleaner than my first draft. So if the claim is about the artifact, I think it's wrong.

What I'd say instead is that the hard part of microGPT was never the typing. The hard part was deciding what to leave out. You've got this enormous space of things you could include. Mixed precision, key-value caching, rotary embeddings, flash attention, all the stuff that makes a real model fast. And every one of those is correct and useful and also completely destroys the thing you're trying to do, which is let somebody hold the entire system in their head at once. So you're making these hundreds of little judgment calls about what's essential versus what's incidental, and each one is a kind of pedagogical bet about where people get confused.

And that's where I think there's a gap right now, not a permanent one. Agents are very good at completing a specification. They're less good at having a strong opinion about what the specification should be when there's no objective metric. There's no loss function for "did this help someone understand attention." You find out by watching people struggle with it for years, by giving lectures and seeing where the faces go blank. microGPT is sort of a compression of all those failed explanations.

The other piece is taste about what's wrong with existing explanations. A lot of the value isn't in what microGPT does, it's in the implicit argument that the other way of explaining it was bad. That's a contrarian stance. Agents today are trained to be agreeable with the distribution of what exists. They'll give you a very good average of how transformers have been taught. They're less likely to say, no, everybody's been doing this backwards, let me show you.

But I want to be honest that this is a snapshot. I don't think there's anything magical here. The models are getting much better at exactly this kind of thing, and I would not be surprised if in a couple of years the best educational code on the internet is agent-written. I'd just say that right now, the scarce resource is still the judgment, not the implementation. And microGPT is mostly judgment wearing a very thin coat of code.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes agents’ ability to produce the code or complete a specification from their weaker ability to decide what the specification should be. It presents microGPT’s simplification as a judgment about what to omit, which agents are less likely to originate today.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish writing the code from deciding that this is the thing worth making. If you tell an agent, “Build a tiny, self-contained GPT implementation,” that’s a fairly concrete task. I wouldn’t claim an agent couldn’t do it.

The interesting part is choosing what to strip away. What’s the smallest version that still captures the idea? Which details are essential, and which are just making it harder to understand? You’re optimizing for a person having that moment of, “Oh, that’s all it is. I understand it now.” That requires a model of the reader, and some taste about how to explain things.

So I’d frame the contribution as identifying and shaping that artifact, rather than producing the individual lines of code. And I don’t think that’s a permanent boundary for AI. It’s just a different capability from solving a well-specified programming task.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes originating and shaping the simplified artifact from carrying out a specified coding task, but it does not say an agent is unable to originate that simplification. It explicitly says this is not a permanent boundary for AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an agent could write the code. The harder part is deciding that this is a thing worth making, and then having a very particular taste for what it should be. How small can you make it? What do you keep so that it still captures the essential idea? What do you remove because it’s just distracting machinery?

With microGPT, the goal is to make something that a person can actually hold in their head. That’s a different objective from just getting an implementation that works. You’re thinking about the reader and the sequence of realizations you want them to have.

So I wouldn’t say an agent fundamentally couldn’t make that contribution. But there’s a difference between asking an agent to implement a small GPT and having it independently recognize that this particular artifact is missing, that it would be valuable, and that this is the right form for it. The code is only part of the contribution.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent could write the code and distinguishes implementation from independently recognizing the artifact’s value and choosing its form. It does not clearly say an agent is unable to originate the simplification; it explicitly says an agent could make the contribution.
